title: The Strategist in the Gray Flannel Suit
gist: Teaser of Beverly Gage's review essay on Bevan Sewell's biography of John Foster Dulles, covering his tenure as Eisenhower's secretary of state and the Cold War consensus.

insights.claim: John Foster Dulles was secretary of state under Eisenhower from 1953 to 1959 and presided over some of the most controversial early Cold War episodes in American foreign policy.
insights.speaker: Beverly Gage
insights.so_what: Anchors the historical case for how U.S. covert statecraft was institutionalized.
insights.locator: John Foster Dulles was the most and least compelling of men

insights.claim: Those episodes included the U.S.-backed coups in Guatemala and Iran, the American break with France, Israel and the United Kingdom during the Suez crisis, and the effort to exploit Khrushchev's secret speech revealing Stalin's crimes.
insights.speaker: Beverly Gage
insights.so_what: Shows the pattern of covert action as a core tool, relevant to reading current U.S. interventions.
insights.locator: the clandestine U.S.-backed coups in Guatemala and Iran

insights.claim: Dulles is portrayed as a man of contradictions, 'the most and least compelling of men', and the text notes a turn to covert action as an essential tool of U.S. policy.
insights.speaker: Beverly Gage
insights.so_what: Covert action as standing instrument is a durable feature of U.S. strategy.
insights.quote: most and least compelling of men
